title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics
book_title: Chapter 3: Inside the $50 Billion Factory & the Gross-to-Net Machine

epigraph.quote: Supply has been our primary constraint, and we are building the largest manufacturing expansion in the history of the pharmaceutical industry to meet global patient demand.
epigraph.author: Lucas Montarce, EVP & CFO, Eli Lilly

web_blocks.html: Eli Lilly sells through two very different paths: the U.S. wholesale-PBM system and a fast-growing direct consumer platform. Over 80% of U.S. volume still moves through three wholesalers: McKesson, Cencora, and Cardinal Health. Meanwhile, three big Pharmacy Benefit Managers (CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, and OptumRx) set net prices. List prices for top incretins and biologics often top $1,000 a month. Yet PBM rebates, 340B hospital cuts, and government rules trim net realized prices by 40% to 60%.

Lilly launched LillyDirect in 2024 and scaled it fast through 2026 to bypass payer friction and fight copycat compounders. The platform links uninsured or denied patients with telehealth doctors. It then ships Zepbound vials and oral Foundayo pills straight to their homes at clear cash prices ($349–$499/month). This direct path cuts out wholesaler and PBM rebates. Even at lower sticker prices, Lilly keeps strong unit margins and gains live demand data.

On the supply side, Lilly is running the largest plant buildout in drug history. From 2020 to early 2025, Lilly pledged over $50 billion for U.S. plants. In February 2025, it added $27 billion for four new sites: three for API synthesis and one for sterile fill-finish, including a $3.5 billion plant in Fogelsville, Pennsylvania. Annual PPE capex jumped from $1,873 million in 2021 to $3,448 million in 2023, $5,058 million in 2024, and $7,841 million in 2025. Oral Foundayo's April 2026 approval also eases long-term pen bottlenecks, since pills need far less capex and cold storage than injectables.

web_blocks.html: Heading into 2027, the key unit-economics test pits volume growth against lower net prices. In Q3 2026, Lilly posted 53% YoY volume growth against a 15% drop in net realized prices. Broader commercial rebates, Medicare deals, and LillyDirect cash tiers drove that price decline. Because gross margins on peptides and oral pills top 80%, strong volume still lifts operating profit. That holds as long as plants stay busy and price cuts do not outrun volume gains.

Lilly's >$50 billion plant network spans Indiana (Indianapolis and Lebanon), North Carolina (Research Triangle Park and Concord), Wisconsin (Kenosha), Pennsylvania (Fogelsville at $3.5 billion), and Limerick, Ireland. New sterile plants take 36 to 60 months to clear FDA cGMP checks from groundbreaking to commercial launch. As a result, Lilly's 2020–2023 projects are hitting full output across 2025–2027. The February 2025 wave of four new U.S. plants ($27 billion) will come online later in the decade for retatrutide, cancer, and immune drugs.

Adding LillyDirect also improves working capital over time. Wholesale orders carry 30-to-60-day payment terms and slow PBM rebate true-ups on the balance sheet. By contrast, LillyDirect cash orders settle right away with no PBM rebate lag.

On costs, peptide synthesis and cell-culture plants gain sharp scale benefits. As new lines in Concord and Limerick shift from test runs to full output, fixed costs spread over more units. That helped push gross margin to 83.04% in FY2025 despite $1,997 million in D&A and rapid global growth.

Still, investors must watch for excess plant spending. If oral Foundayo takes a bigger share of maintenance obesity care, demand could shift from pens to pills. Lilly must pace its late-decade injectable buildout so costly fill-finish lines do not sit idle.

Finally, Lilly's cold-chain and quality record sets it apart. Fast-growing sterile plants often hit FDA Form 483 warnings or recalls. Lilly's automated lines and dual-sourced API sites across North America and Europe have avoided major disruptions while supporting 45%–53% annual volume growth.

Audited footnotes also reveal three unit-economics and concentration frictions. First, FY2025 Form 10-K Note 2 discloses that McKesson, Cencora, and Cardinal Health each accounted for 16% to 24% of consolidated revenue and 20% to 29% each of uncollateralized accounts receivable. Second, Q3 2026 10-Q Note 3 confirms that oral Foundayo carries a mid-single-digit to low-teens tiered royalty to Chugai (and Ebglyss carries a high-single-digit to high-teens royalty to Roche), both booked directly in Cost of Sales—partially offsetting tablet manufacturing savings. Third, ex-U.S. realized net prices fell 29% YoY in Q3 2026 after Mounjaro entered China's National Reimbursement Drug List (NRDL), while Lilly's >$50 billion U.S. manufacturing commitments also serve to secure conditional Section 232 pharmaceutical tariff exemptions.

book_paragraphs: When you and I open a pharmaceutical company's income statement, the first number we see is net revenue—$65,179 million for Eli Lilly in FY2025. But that headline figure hides a tug-of-war that happens before a single dollar is booked: the gross-to-net waterfall. In the United States, a drug's list price is mostly an opening bid. Between the factory loading dock and the patient's medicine cabinet sit three giant wholesalers—McKesson, Cencora, and Cardinal Health—and three dominant Pharmacy Benefit Managers—CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, and OptumRx. To earn preferred formulary placement, Lilly rebates 40% to 60% of list price back to PBMs, insurers, 340B hospitals, and Medicaid.

That is why LillyDirect, launched in 2024 and scaled dramatically through 2026, is such a clever strategic flanking maneuver. By offering single-dose Zepbound vials and, since April 2026, oral Foundayo tablets directly to cash-paying patients for $349 to $499 a month, Lilly cuts out the PBM rebate layer entirely. The patient pays far less than the $1,000+ list price, unauthorized compounding pharmacies lose their price-arbitrage hook, and Lilly still captures software-like unit economics.

Three footnote-level frictions temper the headline unit-economics story. First, Note 2 of the FY2025 10-K reveals that McKesson, Cencora, and Cardinal Health each represent 16% to 24% of consolidated revenue and 20% to 29% of uncollateralized accounts receivable. Second, Q3 2026 10-Q Note 3 discloses that oral Foundayo owes Chugai a mid-single-digit to low-teens tiered royalty inside Cost of Sales, alongside Roche royalties on Ebglyss. Third, Q3 2026 ex-U.S. realized prices dropped 29% YoY following Mounjaro's inclusion on China's NRDL, and Lilly's >$50 billion U.S. CapEx roadmap is explicitly tied to maintaining Section 232 tariff exemptions.

book_subsections.title: The $50 Billion Concrete-and-Steel Moat
paragraphs: Most investors think of pharmaceutical moats purely in terms of patents. At Lilly, the second moat is made of stainless steel, peptide synthesizers, and aseptic fill-finish lines. Since 2020, Lilly has committed over $50 billion to U.S. manufacturing expansion, including a $27 billion commitment in February 2025 for four new domestic sites. Annual PPE capital expenditures nearly quadrupled from $1.87 billion in 2021 to $7.84 billion in 2025.

As CFO Lucas Montarce has explained, building sterile injectable capacity takes three to five years from groundbreaking to FDA inspection. That multi-year physical lead time is why Lilly and Novo Nordisk effectively operated a supply-constrained duopoly through 2024 and 2025. Now, with Foundayo (orforglipron) approved as an oral small-molecule tablet in April 2026, Lilly gains a second, far less capital-intensive manufacturing track—one that can scale to tens of millions of patients globally without cold-chain refrigeration.

book_subsections.title: Tracing Every $100 of FY2025 Revenue
paragraphs: Let's walk through Lilly's audited FY2025 unit economics per $100 of net revenue. Out of $100 collected, Cost of Sales takes just $16.96, leaving $83.04 in gross profit—an 83.04% gross margin that rivals enterprise software. From that $83.04, Lilly reinvests $20.46 into internal R&D ($13,337 million), spends $17.02 on marketing, selling, and administration ($11,094 million), and absorbs $5.21 in acquired IPR&D and restructuring charges ($3,394 million). That leaves $40.35 in operating income ($26,302 million)—a 40.35% operating margin.

After $0.88 in net interest and other expenses and $7.81 in income taxes, Net Income lands at $31.67 per $100 ($20,640 million). On the cash flow statement, working capital expansion to support 45% revenue growth trimmed Operating Cash Flow to $25.80 per $100 ($16,813 million). Subtracting $12.03 in PPE capital expenditures ($7,841 million) still left $13.77 of every $100—nearly $9.0 billion in hard Free Cash Flow—available for dividends, debt service, and buybacks.

callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: Watching the Price-Volume Scissors
callouts.text: In Q3 2026, Lilly's volume jumped 53% while realized net prices fell 15%. As long as volume grows three times faster than price erodes on an 83% gross-margin base, operating profits soar. The moment volume growth slows toward 10% while price erosion stays at -15%, however, that $50 billion fixed-asset base turns from an operating-leverage tailwind into a depreciation headwind.

book_subsections.title: Why Sterile Fill-Finish Takes Five Years to Build
paragraphs: If you have never toured a sterile injectable pharmaceutical plant, it is easy to underestimate why Lilly and Novo Nordisk couldn't simply 'turn up the dial' when demand exploded in 2023. Producing an active peptide ingredient like tirzepatide is only half the battle. The harder bottleneck is aseptic fill-finish: filling microscopic glass cartridges inside Grade A isolators, inspecting them at high speed for particulate defects, assembling spring-loaded auto-injector pens, and validating every single step with the FDA.

From breaking ground on a greenfield site in Concord, North Carolina, or Lebanon, Indiana, to shipping the first commercial box takes three to five years and billions of dollars. That physical lead time is why Lilly's early-mover capex in 2020–2023 became a strategic moat in 2025–2026—and why the $27 billion expansion announced in February 2025 is aimed at locking in capacity for retatrutide and next-generation biologics through the 2030s.

book_subsections.title: Gross-to-Net Realization: The Invisible Income Statement
paragraphs: One of the most important habits you and I can build when analyzing U.S. pharma is looking past list prices to net realization. When Lilly reports $65,179 million in FY2025 revenue, that is net revenue after tens of billions of dollars in gross-to-net deductions: PBM rebates, wholesaler prompt-pay discounts, 340B hospital chargebacks, Medicaid statutory rebates, and Medicare Part D redesign contributions.

In Q3 2026, when Lilly reported 53% volume growth alongside a 15% realized net price decline, that -15% figure did not mean demand was weak; it meant Lilly deliberately traded lower unit prices in exchange for broader commercial formulary coverage, Medicare access agreements, and lower-priced LillyDirect self-pay vials. On an 83% gross margin product, trading 15% on price to capture 53% more volume is a mathematically brilliant trade—as long as manufacturing utilization stays high.

book_subsections.title: The Oral Shift: Protecting Unit Margins When Pills Scale
paragraphs: Think for a moment about what happens to Lilly's supply chain as Foundayo (orforglipron) scales after its April 2026 approval. Injectable tirzepatide requires cold-chain storage at 2°C to 8°C from the factory to the wholesaler to the pharmacy refrigerator to the patient's home. Every step adds freight cost, packaging waste, and spoilage risk. A small-molecule oral tablet like Foundayo sits at room temperature in a blister pack or bottle, costing pennies per dose to package and ship.

That cost advantage is critical as net prices compress. Even if oral GLP-1 therapies are priced 20% to 30% lower than injectable pens to broaden primary-care and international adoption, lower manufacturing and cold-chain costs help defend Lilly's 80%+ gross margin profile. Meanwhile, the company's sterile fill-finish network can pivot toward higher-potency injectables like retatrutide and specialty immunology/neuroscience biologics.

book_subsections.title: Quality Control as an Unseen Moat
paragraphs: In sterile injectable manufacturing, speed without quality control is fatal. A single FDA warning letter or contaminated batch can shut down a fill-finish facility for twelve to eighteen months, handing market share straight to Novo Nordisk or compounders. Lilly's ability to scale volume by 46% in Q4 2025 and 53% in Q3 2026 without a major recall or regulatory plant shutdown is an operational achievement that rarely makes headlines—yet it underpins every dollar of that 83.04% gross margin.

As we move to Chapter 4, keep this physical reality in mind: anyone can draw a peptide on a whiteboard, and dozens of biotechs can run a promising Phase 2 trial, but very few organizations on earth can manufacture, sterilize, package, and distribute hundreds of millions of doses with consistent regulatory compliance.

book_subsections.title: Why Manufacturing Scale Is a Real Economic Moat
paragraphs: In traditional small-molecule pharmaceuticals, manufacturing is an afterthought—you outsource pill pressing to contract manufacturers and focus on marketing. Peptide injectables and sterile pre-filled pens work completely differently. Producing tirzepatide at global scale requires specialized solid-phase and solution-phase synthesis, complex cold-chain logistics, and automated sterile fill-finish lines that take three to five years to permit, build, and validate with the FDA.

By committing more than $50 billion to U.S. manufacturing expansion since 2020 across Indiana, North Carolina, and Wisconsin, Lilly turned a supply bottleneck into a competitive barrier. Every new sterile line lowers unit cost per pen while locking in reliable supply for payers and patients. That is why gross margins expanded past 83% even as Lilly absorbed 15% realized net price declines in Q3 2026.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: Capex as Strategy, Not Waste
book_callouts.text: When a company spends $7.84 billion a year on factories, you and I have to ask whether it is maintenance capex or moat-building capex. At Lilly, every dollar of sterile fill-finish and API capacity serves unmet patient demand that was previously rationed—making this one of the highest-return capital expenditure cycles in modern healthcare, provided demand does not hit an affordability wall.
